groups.title: How Indexes Work Internally
groups.question: Explain how a database index works internally and why it speeds up queries.

followUps.B-Tree Index Structure: Why does a B-tree being sorted help with range queries and ORDER BY, not just exact matches?
followUps.GIN, BRIN & Hash Indexes: When would you use GIN or BRIN instead of a B-tree, and when is BRIN a poor choice?

evidence.text: A B-tree keeps keys in sorted order.
So a range query finds the start and reads forward, instead of scanning everything.
Sorted order also lets ORDER BY read rows already sorted, skipping a sort step.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (B-tree) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a B-tree only helps exact-match lookups.

evidence.text: GIN indexes each element inside arrays, JSONB or text, for containment and full-text searches.
BRIN stores min/max per block range, tiny and great for huge naturally ordered data like time-series.
BRIN is poor when values are scattered randomly across the table.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (GIN, BRIN) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a B-tree is best for every kind of query.

groups.title: Composite & Partial Indexes
groups.question: Walk through how you would design indexes for queries that filter on more than one column.

followUps.Composite Indexes & Column Order: You have an index on (a, b). Which queries can use it, and how do you choose the column order?
followUps.Partial Indexes: When does a partial index beat a full index, and what does it save?

evidence.text: An index on (a, b) helps queries on a, or on a and b, but not on b alone.
Put columns filtered by equality before columns used for ranges.
Choose the order by the queries you run, not by cardinality alone.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (composite index) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

evidence.text: A partial index only covers rows matching a condition.
It wins when queries always target a small subset, like pending rows.
It's smaller, faster to search and cheaper to maintain on writes.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (partial index) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a partial index can serve queries outside its condition.

groups.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE & Query Planning
groups.question: Explain how you figure out why a query is slow.

followUps.Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE Output: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, what does a big gap between estimated and actual rows tell you?
followUps.Seq Scan vs Index Scan vs Index-Only Sca: Why might the planner ignore your index and scan the whole table, and when is an index-only scan possible?

evidence.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the planner's estimated rows next to the real ones.
A big gap means the planner's statistics are wrong or stale.
So the plan is probably bad; run ANALYZE or improve statistics.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the estimated and actual row counts don't matter.

evidence.text: If a query returns a large share of the table, reading it sequentially is cheaper than many index lookups.
So the planner may ignore the index on purpose.
An index-only scan works when the index holds every needed column and the pages are marked all-visible.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (seq scan, index scan) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the planner always uses an index when one exists.

groups.title: Connection Pooling & N+1
groups.question: Walk through common ways an application wastes database round trips and connections.

followUps.The N+1 Query Problem: How do you spot an N+1 query problem in ORM code, and how do you fix it?
followUps.PgBouncer & Connection Pooling: How does PgBouncer let many app connections share a few database connections, and why does that matter for PostgreSQL?

evidence.text: You see one query for the list and then one query per item, e.g. in query logs or as many repeated similar queries.
ORMs cause it by lazily loading a relation inside a loop.
Fix it with eager loading, a join, or one IN query for all ids.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (N+1, ORM) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

evidence.text: PostgreSQL starts a process per connection, so thousands of connections waste memory and CPU.
PgBouncer lets many client connections share a few real ones.
In transaction mode a real connection is held only during a transaction.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (PgBouncer, connection pooling) without explaining how they work or why they matter.
